title: The Board Found Four Contributing Factors in Colgan Air Flight 3407. One of Them Was the Company.
title_candidates: The Board Found Four Contributing Factors in Colgan Air Flight 3407. One of Them Was the Company.
Colgan Air Could Not See Four Things About Flight 3407's Captain. It Moved Him Up Anyway.
Colgan Air Flight 3407 Had Eighteen Seconds of Warning First. Neither Pilot Responded to the Cues.
description:
At seventeen minutes past ten on a February night, a turboprop on approach to Buffalo was five miles from the runway. Everything on board was working.

The warning fired with the wings level and enough speed to fix it. Before it, there were eighteen seconds. It is the only warning on the aeroplane that arrives early, and it arrives silently, and it arrives in the one place a pilot is trained to look.

This is a film about the eighteen seconds, and about the paperwork sixteen years behind them.

It is the twelfth of February, 2009. The aeroplane is a Bombardier Q400, flying as Continental Connection 3407 for a regional carrier called Colgan Air. There are forty-five passengers, two flight attendants and two pilots aboard. Both pilots are based at Newark. Neither of them lives there.

The low-speed cue appeared on the display. The bar began to climb. And nothing happened for eighteen seconds. The cues gave adequate time for the pilots to initiate corrective action, and neither pilot responded to the presence of these cues.

Then the numbers went red and the shaker fired. At that moment the aeroplane was still flying. The wings were level. The load factor was one G. There was enough airspeed available to correct the situation. The captain pulled back on the control column. At about seventeen minutes past ten it came down on a house in Clarence Center, five nautical miles north-east of the airport. Fifty people.

Here is where the easy story arrives, and it is worth taking seriously, because it is half true. A first officer on fifteen thousand eight hundred dollars a year had flown all night across the continent to get to work. A captain with no fixed address near his base had slept in a crew room. Both were tired. The airline had made that normal.

Now hold the Board's sentence beside it. The pilots' performance was likely impaired because of fatigue. But the extent of their impairment, and the degree to which it contributed to the performance deficiencies that occurred during the flight, cannot be conclusively determined. A film that says fatigue did it is more satisfying than the Board and less true.

The probable cause is the captain's inappropriate response to the activation of the stick shaker, which led to an aerodynamic stall from which the airplane did not recover.

On the first of October, 1991, the captain was disapproved for his instrument rating. And on the fifteenth of October, 2007, by now a first officer at Colgan, he was disapproved for his airline transport pilot certificate. Four disapprovals across sixteen years.

Failing a check ride is not rare. In 2008, the overall failure rate for a first attempt at an airline transport pilot certificate was thirteen point one per cent. What matters is not the failures. What matters is who could see them.

Colgan's employment application asked one line. Have you ever failed any proficiency check, FAA check ride, IOE or line check? In 2005 he answered yes, and he described one. At that point he was carrying two other certificate disapprovals. Neither appeared on the form. At the public hearing in May 2009, Colgan's vice-president of administration said that if the captain's incomplete answer had previously been known, it would have resulted in his dismissal from the company. The file that would have contradicted it existed, at the Federal Aviation Administration, the whole time. The systems simply did not talk.

The Board issued its report in February 2010. The four contributing factors were the crew's failure to monitor airspeed, the failure to keep a sterile cockpit, the captain's failure to manage the flight, and Colgan Air's inadequate procedures for airspeed selection and management during approaches in icing conditions.

And in August 2010, Congress passed the Airline Safety and Federal Aviation Administration Extension Act. It required every first officer at a commercial carrier to hold an airline transport pilot certificate. It required safety management systems at commercial air carriers. And it required the Federal Aviation Administration to build a central database of pilot records, kept for the life of a pilot, which an airline must review before it hires.

There is one thing the fifteen-hundred-hour rule does not do, and an honest film has to say it. It would not have changed this flight. The captain already held an airline transport pilot certificate. The headline reform and the useful reform were not the same reform.

—

Prime Documentary makes long-form documentaries about ordinary people and the systems that fail around them. This episode is built from the accident investigation report and the public hearing record. Nothing here states that fatigue caused this accident, because the Board did not.

This film contains AI-assisted visualization: symbolic reconstruction, no real likenesses. Generated imagery is not evidence and is not presented as an authentic record.
